0C0XlULifJtAgn6ZNCW2eu.extract:
The Killers formed in Las Vegas, Nevada in 2001, emerging from a desert city not previously known as an incubator for indie or alternative rock. Frontman Brandon Flowers, a Utah-raised synth-pop devotee, met guitarist Dave Keuning after responding to a classified ad Keuning had placed in a local weekly. The lineup solidified with bassist Mark Stoermer and drummer Ronnie Vannucci Jr., and the band began playing small Vegas clubs like the Junkyard while soaking up the transatlantic post-punk revival then sweeping through New York and London. Their formative touchstones were unmistakable: the anthemic sweep of U2, the arch romanticism of Morrissey and the Smiths, the synth textures of Duran Duran and New Order, and the leather-jacket cool of contemporaries like Interpol and the Strokes.

After being turned down by American labels, the band signed to the London indie Lizard King, with Island handling the U.S. release, and issued their debut Hot Fuss in 2004. Built around the singles Mr. Brightside, Somebody Told Me, All These Things That I've Done, and Smile Like You Mean It, the record fused new wave keyboards with muscular guitar hooks and Flowers's theatrical delivery, becoming one of the defining alternative albums of the decade. Mr. Brightside in particular achieved a near-mythic afterlife, charting in the UK for a record-shattering number of consecutive weeks and becoming a karaoke and stadium staple long after its release.

For 2006's Sam's Town, produced by Flood and Alan Moulder, the band pivoted sharply toward heartland Americana, invoking Bruce Springsteen and Tom Petty in tracks like When You Were Young and the title cut. The pivot puzzled some critics at the time but has aged into one of their most beloved statements, with Read My Mind emerging as a fan favorite. Day & Age (2008), produced by Stuart Price, swung back to synths and disco pulse with Human and Spaceman, while 2012's Battle Born aimed for widescreen rock ambition. Along the way Flowers pursued a solo career with Flamingo and The Desired Effect, and the band contributed to holiday charity singles and various one-off collaborations, including work with New Order's Bernard Sumner and Pet Shop Boys touchstones that reinforced their British new-wave lineage.

Later albums Wonderful Wonderful (2017), Imploding the Mirage (2020), and Pressure Machine (2021) saw the group working with producers like Jacknife Lee and Shawn Everett, with Imploding the Mirage in particular winning strong reviews for its widescreen, Fleetwood Mac–inflected rock. Pressure Machine, written during the pandemic, was a quieter, narrative-driven record rooted in Flowers's memories of small-town Nephi, Utah, and featured a guest turn from Phoebe Bridgers. Keuning and Stoermer stepped back from touring during this period, though they remained connected to the band.

Critically, The Killers occupy a rare position: a stadium-filling rock act whose signature song keeps gaining cultural velocity nearly two decades after release, and whose catalog spans glossy synth-pop, Americana, and gospel-tinged arena rock. They continue to tour globally, headlining festivals like Glastonbury, and stand as the most commercially successful rock band Las Vegas has ever produced, a legacy sealed by Hot Fuss's enduring ubiquity.
0C0XlULifJtAgn6ZNCW2eu.title: The Killers

0ECwFtbIWEVNwjlrfc6xoL.extract:
The Eagles formed in Los Angeles in 1971, emerging from the fertile country-rock scene that had taken root around clubs like the Troubadour in the late 1960s. The original lineup consisted of Glenn Frey on guitar and vocals, Don Henley on drums and vocals, Bernie Leadon on guitar and banjo, and Randy Meisner on bass. All four had cut their teeth as backing musicians for Linda Ronstadt, and that experience cemented the harmonic blend and laid-back groove that would define their early sound. They signed to David Geffen's newly formed Asylum Records, which positioned them alongside labelmates like Jackson Browne, Joni Mitchell, and J.D. Souther, the latter of whom became a frequent co-writer.

Their self-titled 1972 debut, recorded in London with producer Glyn Johns, yielded the singles Take It Easy (co-written with Browne), Witchy Woman, and Peaceful Easy Feeling, establishing them immediately as commercial force in the country-rock idiom. The 1973 concept album Desperado, also produced by Johns, drew on Old West imagery and contained the title track and Tequila Sunrise, though it sold modestly at first. With On the Border in 1974, the band shifted toward a harder rock direction, parted ways with Johns mid-project in favor of Bill Szymczyk, and added guitarist Don Felder. That move paid off with One of These Nights in 1975, which produced the chart-topping title track along with Lyin' Eyes and Take It to the Limit.

Leadon departed at the end of the One of These Nights tour and was replaced by Joe Walsh, formerly of the James Gang, whose harder-edged guitar work pushed the band fully into mainstream rock territory. The result was Hotel California in 1976, again produced by Szymczyk, an album that sold in the tens of millions and yielded the title track, New Kid in Town, and Life in the Fast Lane. By this point Henley and Frey had become the dominant creative voices, and tensions within the group escalated during the protracted recording of The Long Run, released in 1979. That record produced Heartache Tonight and the title track but proved to be their last studio album for nearly three decades; the band fractured during a 1980 tour and broke up shortly after.

The 1980s saw Henley and Frey pursue successful solo careers, with Henley releasing The End of the Innocence and Frey scoring hits like The Heat Is On. The Eagles famously vowed to reunite only when "hell freezes over," which they did in 1994 with the live album and tour of that name, featuring new studio cuts including Get Over It and Love Will Keep Us Alive. Meisner had long since been replaced by Timothy B. Schmit, and that lineup eventually produced Long Road Out of Eden in 2007, sold exclusively at first through Walmart, which debuted at number one in the United States.

Glenn Frey died in January 2016, and the band has since toured with his son Deacon Frey and country artist Vince Gill sharing his vocal parts. They mounted extensive Hotel California tours performing the album in full, and have more recently been engaged in a long farewell tour billed as The Long Goodbye. Their cultural footprint is enormous: Their Greatest Hits 1971-1975 stands as one of the best-selling albums in American history, and their fusion of harmony-driven country-rock with arena-rock ambition shaped the sound of mainstream American radio for a generation.
0ECwFtbIWEVNwjlrfc6xoL.title: Eagles

0EeQBlQJFiAfJeVN2vT9s0.extract:
Nipsey Hussle, born Ermias Joseph Asghedom on August 15, 1985, was a rapper and entrepreneur from the Crenshaw district of South Los Angeles. Of Eritrean and African American descent, he came up affiliated with the Rollin' 60s Neighborhood Crips, a reality that shaped both his lyrics and his community-focused worldview. Active from the mid-2000s until his death in 2019, he became one of the defining voices of West Coast independent hip-hop in the 2010s, balancing street narratives with a sharp business mind and a Pan-African political consciousness inherited in part from his father's Eritrean roots.

He emerged through the Los Angeles mixtape circuit in the late 2000s, initially gaining traction with the Bullets Ain't Got No Name series before signing briefly to Epic Records and then Cinematic Music Group. Early influences included Snoop Dogg, Jay-Z, Tupac, and the entrepreneurial template of No Limit and Cash Money, while sonically he drew on the G-funk lineage of his city. His 2010 mixtape The Marathon and its 2011 sequel The Marathon Continues established his signature franchise — a metaphor for endurance, slow-build success, and self-determination — and tracks like "Hussle in the House" and "Bullets Ain't Got No Name" cemented his local legend.

His most discussed release before his debut album was Crenshaw in 2013, which he sold for $100 a copy in a strategy he called "Proud2Pay"; Jay-Z famously bought 100 copies. He followed with Mailbox Money in 2014 under similar terms. Throughout this period he ran his own imprint, All Money In No Money Out, eventually striking a partnership with Atlantic Records for his long-awaited studio debut Victory Lap in 2018. The album, featuring collaborators like YG, Kendrick Lamar, Diddy, CeeLo Green, and production from the likes of Mike & Keys and Mars of 1500 or Nothin', was nominated for Best Rap Album at the Grammys and is widely considered the culmination of a decade of independent grinding.

Beyond music, Nipsey was deeply invested in Crenshaw as a place. He co-founded Vector90, a coworking space and STEM incubator for Black youth, opened the Marathon Clothing smart store on Slauson Avenue, and invested in local real estate alongside his brother Samiel "Blacc Sam" Asghedom. He spoke frequently about ownership, generational wealth, and the failures of the music industry's traditional contracts, becoming a touchstone for a generation of artists rethinking distribution. His friendships and collaborations with YG (most prominently on the 2016 protest single "FDT"), Dom Kennedy, Snoop Dogg, and Roddy Ricch tied him into the fabric of contemporary L.A. rap.

On March 31, 2019, Nipsey was shot and killed outside the Marathon store; he was 33. The response was extraordinary — a memorial at the Staples Center, tributes from Barack Obama, and a posthumous sweep at the 2020 Grammys, where "Racks in the Middle" with Roddy Ricch and Hit-Boy won Best Rap Performance and "Higher," his collaboration with DJ Khaled and John Legend, won Best Rap/Sung Performance. His legacy lives on through the Marathon brand, the Nipsey Hussle Fellowship, and an enduring influence on artists who treat rap as a vehicle for ownership, neighborhood investment, and long-game thinking rather than quick stardom.
0EeQBlQJFiAfJeVN2vT9s0.title: Nipsey Hussle

0IcwumPFXL1XWQ0Z9CCuCV.extract:
Broder Daniel was an indie rock band from Gothenburg, Sweden, active from 1989 until 2008. They became one of the defining acts of the city's indie scene, a cult band whose bruised, romantic songs about alienation, longing and adolescent outsiderdom made them a touchstone for a generation of Swedish listeners. Though they never had broad commercial success abroad, their devoted following at home turned them into something close to a mythology, particularly in Gothenburg.

The band formed around singer and songwriter Henrik Berggren, whose fragile, strained vocal delivery and diaristic English-language lyrics became the group's signature. The lineup shifted over the years and included guitarist Anders Göthberg, bassist Daniel Gilbert and, for a period in the mid-1990s, a young Håkan Hellström, who later became one of Sweden's biggest pop stars as a solo artist. Berggren drew openly on British guitar pop and post-punk, especially the melancholic, literate tradition of The Smiths and their contemporaries. That influence shaped the band's mix of jangling guitars, anthemic choruses and confessional melodrama.

Their debut album, Saturday Night Engine (1995), introduced the band's raw, slightly ragged sound. The self-titled follow-up Broder Daniel (1996) consolidated their reputation in Sweden. Their profile rose sharply in 1998, when director Lukas Moodysson used their music prominently in his acclaimed film Fucking Åmål (released internationally as Show Me Love). The film tells the story of two teenage girls falling in love in a stifling small town, and the song I'll Be Gone became closely associated with it, as did the companion release Songs From The Movie Fucking Åmål. The same year brought Broder Daniel Forever, often regarded as their emotional high point. The release Happy People Never Fantasize followed in 1999.

After a lengthy gap, the band returned with Cruel Town (2003), a darker and more polished record preceded by the single When We Were Winning. The single Shoreline followed in 2004 and became perhaps their most beloved song, a sweeping anthem that remains a staple at Swedish indie club nights and singalongs. In this later period the band's sound grew fuller, with guitarist Theodor Jensen contributing to the lineup.

In 2008 Anders Göthberg died, and the band decided to end its career. Broder Daniel played a farewell concert at the Way Out West festival in Gothenburg that August, an emotional performance before a huge hometown crowd that cemented their legend. The 2010 compilation Big-5 : Broder Daniel gathered key material for new listeners.

The band's legacy lives on through its members and its influence. Håkan Hellström's enormous success kept the Broder Daniel lineage in the public eye, Theodor Jensen continued with his own projects, and Berggren eventually returned with solo work, including the album Wolf's Heart in 2016. Broder Daniel is remembered as the archetypal Gothenburg indie band: earnest, wounded and fiercely loved, a group whose songs gave voice to Swedish teenagers who felt they didn't fit in.
0IcwumPFXL1XWQ0Z9CCuCV.title: Broder Daniel

0Repe2EiNjaFAFIukrroUM.extract:
Ren, born Ren Gill in 1990, is a Welsh singer, rapper, and multi-instrumentalist who grew up in Brighton, England after being born in Bangor, Wales. He first began performing in the late 2000s, busking on Brighton's streets and playing in the acoustic duo The Big Push with Sam Tompkins around 2010-2012. That early period saw him signed to Sony in his early twenties, but his career was derailed when he became severely ill with what was eventually diagnosed, many years later, as Lyme disease alongside autoimmune complications and psychological struggles. He spent much of the following decade largely offline, battling chronic illness, which became a defining thread in both his personal narrative and his songwriting.

His formative influences span a remarkably wide range — hip hop, folk, blues, singer-songwriter traditions, and theatrical storytelling — and this eclecticism became his signature rather than a liability. Ren is essentially a self-contained artist, writing, producing, and performing his own material, often filming stripped-down performances in his home. After years of dormancy he began uploading music and acoustic videos to YouTube, and the platform, rather than any label push, became the engine of his second act. Tracks like Money Game (and its sequels) gained traction for their rapid-fire verses and pointed critiques of capitalism and mental health, but it was Hi Ren, released in 2022, that transformed his career: a nearly seven-minute dialogue between two sides of himself, alternating between rapped verses and acoustic guitar passages, that went viral and drew millions of viewers into his back catalogue.

On the momentum of Hi Ren, he released the full-length Sick Boi in 2023, an autobiographical record built around his years of illness, followed by the more expansive Sick Boi (Deluxe) and then the 2024 album The Tale of Jenny & Screech, a narrative concept work told across interconnected tracks. He also collaborated with fellow British artist Chinchilla on the single Chalk Outlines in 2023, which became one of his most-streamed songs and reached the UK singles chart. His work has been released independently through his own imprint, The Other Songs having supported some earlier distribution, giving him near-total creative control — a rarity for an artist operating at his scale of audience.

Critical reception has tended to focus on the emotional directness and structural ambition of his songs rather than genre placement, since he moves between rap, folk balladry, spoken word, and rock within single tracks. He has become something of a figurehead for artists who bypass traditional industry gatekeeping, and his transparent discussion of chronic illness, medical gaslighting, and mental health has given him a devoted listener base that treats his releases as events. Fellow independent-minded UK acts and the wider YouTube singer-songwriter ecosystem, including his old collaborator Sam Tompkins, share adjacent territory.

Currently, Ren continues to release music and long-form videos to his growing YouTube following while managing his ongoing health issues, which have at times forced him to cancel touring plans. His legacy, still being written, is already notable as a case study in artistic reinvention outside the major-label system and in the viability of deeply personal, formally ambitious songwriting reaching a mass audience through direct-to-fan channels.
0Repe2EiNjaFAFIukrroUM.title: Ren

0iqgjl0OG3z53PZVIB7ZyD.extract:
Víkingur Ólafsson is an Icelandic pianist born in Reykjavík in 1984, and since the late 2000s he has become one of the most prominent figures in contemporary classical piano. He grew up in a musical household. His mother, Svana Víkingsdóttir, was a piano teacher, and his father, Ólafur Óskar Axelsson, an architect who also composed. That environment shaped his early sense that performing and composing are closely linked. After his early training in Iceland he moved to New York to study at the Juilliard School, where he earned both his bachelor's and master's degrees.

Back in Iceland, Víkingur Ólafsson took an independent route. He founded his own label, Dirrindí, which released his first two albums: Debut in 2009 and Chopin - Bach in 2011. The second paired Chopin with Bach, a juxtaposition of eras that foreshadowed his later programming. He also founded the Reykjavík Midsummer Music festival in 2012 and presented classical music on Icelandic television, building a public profile at home before his international breakthrough.

That breakthrough came when he signed with Deutsche Grammophon. His first album for the label, Philip Glass: Piano Works (2017), presented Glass's études and other pieces with unusual clarity and rhythmic precision, and included arrangements with string quartet. The same year he played piano on Dario Marianelli's score for the film Darkest Hour. In 2018 came Johann Sebastian Bach, an album mixing original keyboard works with transcriptions, including his own arrangements and Alexander Siloti's B minor reworking of the Prelude in E minor, BWV 855. It became one of the most acclaimed Bach recordings of its time.

The Bach project expanded into Bach Reworks (Pts. 1 and 2, 2018–2019), in which composers and producers, among them Ryuichi Sakamoto, reimagined material from the album. In 2018 he also released For Jóhann, a tribute to his compatriot, the composer Jóhann Jóhannsson, who had died earlier that year. In 2020 he returned with Debussy – Rameau, which set the two French composers side by side. The album included his own transcription The Arts and the Hours, drawn from Rameau's Les Boréades, along with Les tendres plaintes and Debussy's La fille aux cheveux de lin. Again it was followed by a rework, as the Polish pianist-composer Hania Rani reimagined La damoiselle élue.

Critics have praised his intellectual approach to programming and his crystalline, carefully voiced tone. Gramophone named him its Artist of the Year in 2019, and the Johann Sebastian Bach album won major prizes, including BBC Music Magazine recognition. The New York Times called him "Iceland's Glenn Gould," a comparison that captured his blend of rigor and individuality. His readiness to work with electronic and crossover musicians has made him a bridge between the classical mainstream and the Nordic post-classical scene.

Since then he has continued on an ambitious path. Mozart & Contemporaries (2021) and From Afar (2022) were followed by Bach's Goldberg Variations (2023), which he took on an extensive world tour and which won the Grammy for Best Classical Instrumental Solo. He has also championed new repertoire, notably giving the premiere of John Adams's piano concerto After the Fall. He remains a defining classical pianist of his generation.
0iqgjl0OG3z53PZVIB7ZyD.title: Víkingur Ólafsson

0nnYdIpahs41QiZ9MWp5Wx.extract:
Holly Humberstone is an English singer-songwriter from Grantham, Lincolnshire, who emerged in the late 2010s as one of the most distinctive new voices in British alternative pop. Raised in a rambling, slightly dilapidated house with three sisters, she has often cited the rural, isolated quality of her upbringing as central to the introspective, diaristic character of her songwriting. She began writing and uploading music while still a teenager, and by the turn of the decade had been picked up by Polydor Records' Darkroom imprint in the UK, aligning her with a wave of confessional British pop contemporaries including Phoebe Bridgers' broader sphere of influence and peers like Sigrid and Maisie Peters.

Her breakthrough came with the 2020 single Falling Asleep at the Wheel, a fragile, synth-tinged ballad that became the title track of her debut EP later that year. The EP introduced the production partnership that would define much of her early catalogue: her work with producer Rob Milton (formerly of Dog Is Dead), whose lo-fi, textural approach complemented her cracked, intimate vocals and piano-led writing. Songs like Overkill, Drop Dead and Deep End established her template of dryly observed heartbreak and family vignettes set against muted electronic arrangements. The recognition was swift: she was longlisted for the BBC Sound of 2021 poll and won the Rising Star award at the 2022 BRIT Awards.

A second EP, The Walls Are Way Too Thin, arrived in late 2021, sharpening her songwriting on tracks like Scarlet, a sinewy, frustrated meditation on a friend's relationship that became one of her most beloved songs. Around this period she was hand-picked by Olivia Rodrigo to open the UK and European dates of the Sour Tour, dramatically expanding her audience, and she also toured with Lewis Capaldi. A collaboration with The 1975's Matty Healy and George Daniel produced the standalone single Please Don't Leave Just Yet in 2021, cementing her connections to the broader Dirty Hit and Polydor-adjacent British indie-pop ecosystem.

Her debut album Paint My Bedroom Black followed in October 2023, expanding her sonic palette with contributions from Daniel and Healy alongside Milton. Tracks like Antichrist, Into Your Room and the title song pushed her further toward atmospheric, slightly abrasive textures while retaining the conversational lyricism that drew listeners in the first place. Critics broadly welcomed the record as a confident step up from the EPs, even if some felt it lacked a single defining moment to match Scarlet. The album consolidated her standing as a thoughtful, literate songwriter rather than a chart-chasing pop act, and she continued to tour it extensively through 2024, including supporting Girl in Red and headlining her own dates across the UK, Europe and North America.

Humberstone remains an active and rising figure in British alternative pop, working primarily within the orbit of Darkroom and Polydor while maintaining the homespun, songwriter-first identity that distinguished her early work. Her legacy at this still-early stage is as one of the key British artists who helped define a strain of millennial and Gen Z confessional pop in the early 2020s, bridging the bedroom-pop intimacy of the streaming era with a more traditional singer-songwriter craft.
0nnYdIpahs41QiZ9MWp5Wx.title: Holly Humberstone

0vEsuISMWAKNctLlUAhSZC.extract:
Counting Crows formed in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1991, emerging from the Berkeley and San Francisco club circuit and remaining active ever since. The band grew out of a partnership between singer and songwriter Adam Duritz and guitarist David Bryson, who began performing as an acoustic duo before expanding into a full group. Early members included keyboardist Charlie Gillingham, bassist Matt Malley and drummer Steve Bowman. The band took its name from a line in a traditional counting rhyme about magpies, which equates their number with sorrow or joy.

Musically, the band drew openly on Van Morrison, The Band and R.E.M., blending folk-rock warmth with Duritz's confessional, densely detailed lyrics. Signed to DGC, a Geffen imprint, they recorded their debut, August and Everything After (1993), with producer T Bone Burnett. The album broke big on the strength of "Mr. Jones," a wry meditation on fame and longing, followed by the singles "Rain King" and "Omaha," while the sprawling "Round Here" became a fan touchstone. A high-profile appearance on Saturday Night Live helped propel the record to multi-platinum sales. That same era, the band performed Van Morrison's "Caravan" with Robbie Robertson when Morrison was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, underscoring their roots-rock lineage. Guitarist Dan Vickrey joined during this period, and drummer Ben Mize replaced Bowman.

Recovering the Satellites (1996), produced by Gil Norton, was a louder, more anxious record that grappled with sudden celebrity. It entered the Billboard 200 at number one and yielded "Angels of the Silences," the piano ballad "A Long December," and "Daylight Fading." The live set Across a Wire: Live in New York City followed in 1998. This Desert Life (1999), co-produced by David Lowery and Dennis Herring, struck a looser, sunnier tone, led by the upbeat "Hanginaround." Hard Candy (2002), produced by Steve Lillywhite, brought polished pop-rock with "American Girls," featuring backing vocals from Sheryl Crow. The album's cover of Joni Mitchell's "Big Yellow Taxi," featuring Vanessa Carlton, became a radio hit.

The band's widest exposure came with "Accidentally in Love," written for the Shrek 2 soundtrack in 2004, which earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song. Situated alongside the mid-1990s wave of melodic, roots-conscious rock acts that followed grunge, Counting Crows were sometimes grouped with post-grunge and adult-alternative radio. Their narrative songwriting and Duritz's emotive delivery, however, set them apart and drew both devoted fans and skeptics who found the earnestness overwrought. Duritz later spoke publicly about living with a dissociative disorder, adding context to the alienation running through many of his lyrics.

After Saturday Nights and Sunday Mornings (2008), the band left Geffen. They issued the covers album Underwater Sunshine (2012) independently, then released Somewhere Under Wonderland (2014). The four-song Butter Miracle, Suite One (2021) marked a return to ambitious, interconnected songwriting. Counting Crows continue to tour extensively, and their debut remains a defining document of 1990s American rock.
0vEsuISMWAKNctLlUAhSZC.title: Counting Crows

0vtjXmCLNmJti4fJ5dBhxc.extract:
André De Shields is an American actor, singer, director, and choreographer whose recorded presence on Spotify comes almost entirely from Broadway cast albums. Born on January 12, 1946, in Baltimore, Maryland, he has worked on stage for more than five decades. He is best known to contemporary listeners as Hermes, the silver-suited narrator of Anaïs Mitchell's Hadestown. The tracks listed under his name, including Road to Hell, its reprise, Wait for Me, and the spoken intros and outros, come from that show's 2019 Original Broadway Cast Recording.

De Shields was one of eleven children and grew up in segregated Baltimore. He later studied at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. His early theatrical education came partly through Chicago's countercultural scene, where he appeared in a production of Hair at the end of the 1960s. The exuberant, rock-inflected style of that era, along with the Black vaudeville and jazz traditions he absorbed, shaped a performing persona built on elegance, showmanship, and an unmistakably rich speaking voice.

His Broadway breakthrough came in 1975, when he created the title role in The Wiz, Charlie Smalls's soul-and-funk reimagining of The Wizard of Oz. In 1978 he joined the original cast of Ain't Misbehavin', the Fats Waller revue conceived by Richard Maltby Jr. The show became a landmark of the decade, and De Shields won an Emmy Award for the televised version broadcast on NBC in 1982. He conceived and starred in Harlem Nocturne in the 1980s. He earned Tony nominations for Play On!, a Duke Ellington musical set in Harlem, and for The Full Monty in 2000, where his character Noah "Horse" T. Simmons stopped the show with the number "Big Black Man." Across these roles he became a link between the jazz-age songbook and modern musical theater.

Hadestown gave De Shields his most widely heard recordings. Directed by Rachel Chavkin, with orchestrations by Michael Chorney and Todd Sickafoose, the folk-and-New-Orleans-jazz retelling of the Orpheus and Eurydice myth casts Hermes as a sly master of ceremonies. On the cast album he opens the show with Road to Hell, sets up scenes in spoken intros such as When the Chips are Down, and delivers the gentle, fatherly guidance of Wait for Me. He shared the stage with Reeve Carney, Eva Noblezada, Amber Gray, and Patrick Page. The cast recording won the Grammy Award for Best Musical Theater Album.

The role finally brought him a Tony Award in 2019, for Best Featured Actor in a Musical. His acceptance speech became widely quoted for its "three cardinal rules on sustaining longevity in this business":

1. Surround yourself with people whose eyes light up when they see you coming.
2. Slowly is the fastest way to get to where you want to be.
3. The top of one mountain is the bottom of the next, so keep climbing.

The speech, together with his age and decades of persistence, turned the moment into one of the ceremony's most celebrated.

De Shields's legacy spans roughly half a century of Black musical theater, from The Wiz and Ain't Misbehavin' to Hadestown. He has continued to work as a performer, teacher, and speaker, and he is regarded as an elder statesman of Broadway whose career demonstrates the endurance he described in that speech.
0vtjXmCLNmJti4fJ5dBhxc.title: André De Shields

0yNLKJebCb8Aueb54LYya3.extract:
New Order formed in 1980 in Salford, Greater Manchester, England, rising from the wreckage of Joy Division after singer Ian Curtis died in May of that year. Guitarist Bernard Sumner, bassist Peter Hook and drummer Stephen Morris carried on, and Sumner reluctantly took over vocals. Keyboardist and guitarist Gillian Gilbert, Morris's partner, joined later in 1980. The band has been active, with breaks, from then to the present day. Over that time they became one of the defining links between post-punk, synthpop and dance music.

Their early work still carried Joy Division's shadow. The debut single Ceremony (1981) was a song written in Joy Division's final days. The album Movement (1981) was produced by Martin Hannett, and its dense, melancholy sound echoed Closer. The members were absorbing other influences, though. They encountered New York club culture, Giorgio Moroder's electronic disco and Kraftwerk, and they began building a sound around sequencers and drum machines. Everything's Gone Green (1981) and Temptation (1982) marked the turn. Both were driving and pulse-based, and they were self-produced.

That shift peaked with Blue Monday (1983), a nearly seven-minute 12-inch single built on a programmed Oberheim drum pattern and a sequenced synth bass line. It became famous as one of the best-selling 12-inch singles ever. Peter Saville's die-cut sleeve, designed to resemble a floppy disk, was so costly to make that Factory reportedly lost money on each copy. Power, Corruption & Lies (1983) arrived the same year. It paired icy electronics with Hook's high melodic bass on tracks like Age of Consent and The Village. The band then worked with New York producer Arthur Baker on Confusion (1983), steeping themselves in electro and the Funhouse club scene. Thieves Like Us (1984) and Murder (1984) followed, and Low-Life (1985) refined the formula with The Perfect Kiss and Sub-culture. Later albums included Brotherhood (1986), Technique (1989), which was partly recorded in Ibiza, and Republic (1993). Singles such as True Faith (1987), produced with Stephen Hague, and Bizarre Love Triangle gave them transatlantic success.

The band was central to Tony Wilson's Factory Records. Their earnings helped fund the Haçienda, the Manchester club that opened in 1982 and later became a hub of acid house and the Madchester era alongside Happy Mondays. That financial burden contributed to Factory's collapse in 1992, after which New Order moved to London Records. Members also pursued side projects. Sumner formed Electronic with Johnny Marr, Hook formed Revenge and Monaco, and Morris and Gilbert recorded as The Other Two. In 1990 the band recorded World in Motion with the England football squad, which reached number one in the UK.

Critics regard New Order as pioneers who fused rock band dynamics with club electronics. Their influence runs through The Killers, LCD Soundsystem and countless indie-dance acts. After Get Ready (2001) and Waiting for the Sirens' Call (2005), Hook left the band acrimoniously. The others regrouped with Tom Chapman on bass and Gilbert back in the lineup, releasing Music Complete (2015) on Mute. Their catalogue has since been reissued in Definitive Edition boxes, and they continue to tour internationally.
0yNLKJebCb8Aueb54LYya3.title: New Order

193FjJQXUrDge7V3ZqJBO4.extract:
Blå Tåget was a Stockholm group and one of the most literate and idiosyncratic bands of the Swedish progg movement, the politically engaged, Swedish-language alternative scene that flourished from the late 1960s through the 1970s. The band emerged around 1969 and was most active in the first half of the 1970s. Its members later reconvened in the 1980s and again around the turn of the millennium, so the group's history stretches across several decades.

The band grew out of a circle of Stockholm writers, artists and musicians rather than from the conventional rock circuit. Its core included the poet and critic Leif Nylén, Tore Berger, Torkel Rasmusson, Mats G Bengtsson and Kjell Westling. They first recorded under the name Gunder Hägg, a joking reference to the celebrated Swedish runner, and released their debut on the independent label Silence Records. After objections to the use of the athlete's name, they renamed themselves Blå Tåget. From the start their approach mixed amateur enthusiasm, art-world irony and sharp political wit, and they drew as much on cabaret, jazz and Swedish song traditions as on rock.

Brustna hjärtans hotell, released in 1972, is the record most closely associated with the band. Its best-known song is Staten och kapitalet, a pointed critique of the state and capital alike, with lyrics by Nylén. Slowfox followed in 1974 and continued the group's blend of wry lyrical observation and loose, eclectic arrangements. A live document, Blå Tåget på Fågel blå, appeared in 1982 and captured the reunited band in a Stockholm setting. Later studio work came with Moderna Material in 1999 and I tidens rififi in 2004, showing the group's older members still writing in the same ironic, intellectually restless vein.

Blå Tåget belonged to the Silence-centred independent network that defined much of Swedish progg, alongside the festival culture and alternative distribution that sustained the movement outside the commercial industry. Within that scene they stood apart for their literary sensibility, which owed much to Nylén's background in poetry and criticism. Their politics were also less dogmatic and more skeptical than those of many of their peers.

The band's cultural footprint grew far beyond its original audience when the punk group Ebba Grön recorded Staten och kapitalet in the early 1980s. Their version turned the song into one of the most widely known Swedish rock anthems and introduced Blå Tåget's writing to a new generation. The song has since been sung and referenced so widely that it is often regarded as a standard of Swedish protest music.

Archival interest in the band has continued. Melodisk Rock (Live) and Progglådan Blå Tåget (Live från SvR Tonkraft, 1977), both issued in 2013, preserved concert performances from their heyday. Leif Nylén died in 2016. Blå Tåget is remembered as one of the progg era's most intelligent voices, a band whose ironic, questioning songs outlasted the movement that produced them.
193FjJQXUrDge7V3ZqJBO4.title: Blå Tåget

1bgyxtWjZwA5PQlDsvs9b8.extract:
Sarah Vaughan was born on March 27, 1924, in Newark, New Jersey, and became one of the defining voices of American jazz from the mid-1940s until her death in 1990. Nicknamed "Sassy" and "The Divine One," she grew up singing and playing piano and organ at Mount Zion Baptist Church, where her father was a carpenter and amateur guitarist and her mother sang in the choir. Newark's church and club culture gave her a thorough musical grounding, and she took formal piano lessons as a child.

Her break came in 1942 when she won an amateur night contest at Harlem's Apollo Theater. That led to a job with Earl Hines's big band in 1943, alongside Billy Eckstine, Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker. When Eckstine formed his own bebop-oriented orchestra, Vaughan followed him. Immersion in the harmonic language of Parker and Gillespie shaped her approach: she phrased like an instrumentalist and handled chromatic lines with ease. Her 1945 recording of "Lover Man" with Gillespie and Parker is a landmark of early bebop vocals. Later in the decade she recorded for Musicraft, with sides such as "Tenderly" and "It's Magic," then moved to Columbia, where she worked with string orchestras.

The 1950s brought her most celebrated period. Vaughan signed a dual arrangement with Mercury Records, which issued her pop-oriented material, and its jazz subsidiary EmArcy. Her 1954 EmArcy album Sarah Vaughan featured trumpeter Clifford Brown and is widely regarded as one of the great vocal jazz records. Her pop side brought hits including "Make Yourself Comfortable," "Whatever Lola Wants," "Broken-Hearted Melody," and "Misty." Albums from this era show her range: In The Land Of Hi-Fi (1955), with Cannonball Adderley in the ensemble; the intimate After Hours (1955); Sarah Vaughan Sings George Gershwin (1957), arranged by Hal Mooney; Swingin' Easy (1957), with a small trio; and the live Sarah Vaughan At Mister Kelly's (1957), recorded at the Chicago club. No Count Sarah (1958) paired her with members of the Count Basie band. Vaughan And Violins (1958) was arranged by Quincy Jones in Paris. After Hours At The London House (1958) captured her in another Chicago room. By 1960 she had moved to Roulette Records, where Dreamy and The Divine Sarah Vaughan continued her lush ballad work.

Throughout her career Vaughan was often discussed alongside Ella Fitzgerald and Billie Holiday as one of the three great female jazz singers. Her own contribution was operatic: a contralto range spanning nearly three octaves, rich vibrato, and daring improvisational leaps. Her accompanists over the years included pianists Jimmy Jones, Roy Haynes on drums, and later trios with players such as Jimmy Rowles. In later decades she recorded for Mainstream and then Norman Granz's Pablo label, producing albums such as How Long Has This Been Going On? with Oscar Peterson. Her 1982 Gershwin Live!, with Michael Tilson Thomas, earned her a Grammy Award.

Vaughan received the NEA Jazz Masters honor in 1989 and a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award posthumously. She died of lung cancer on April 3, 1990, in Los Angeles. Her recordings remain essential study material for jazz vocalists, and her interpretations of "Misty," "Send in the Clowns" and "Lullaby of Birdland" are still treated as definitive. Her influence is audible in singers ranging from Carmen McRae's successors to contemporary artists like Cécile McLorin Salvant.
1bgyxtWjZwA5PQlDsvs9b8.title: Sarah Vaughan

1tZ99AnqyjgrmPwLfGU5eo.extract:
Fito y Fitipaldis is the band led by Adolfo "Fito" Cabrales, a singer, guitarist and songwriter from Bilbao in the Basque Country. Cabrales was already well known as the frontman of Platero y Tú, one of the defining groups of the hard-edged Basque and Spanish rock scene of the 1990s. He launched Fito y Fitipaldis in 1998 as a side outlet for songs that did not fit Platero's electric, riff-driven style. Over the following years the project became his main vehicle, and it has remained active from the late 1990s into the 2020s.

The project grew from Cabrales's affection for roots rock, soul and blues, the strain of music running from the Rolling Stones to Spanish street-rock figures such as Rosendo. Within the Basque scene he also had close ties to Robe Iniesta of Extremoduro, with whom he formed the one-off project Extrechinato y Tú. The debut, A Puerta Cerrada (1998), introduced a looser, warmer sound built on piano, saxophone and slide guitar. Saxophonist Javier Alzola became a signature voice of the band, and guitarist and producer Carlos Raya became Cabrales's key creative partner.

Los Sueños Locos (2001) arrived around the time Platero y Tú wound down, and songs like "La casa por el tejado" signalled that the band was ready to stand on its own. The commercial breakthrough came with Lo más lejos a tu lado, home to "Soldadito marinero," which became one of the most widely sung Spanish rock songs of the decade. The live album Vivo... para contarlo captured the band's growing stadium-level following. Por la boca vive el pez (2006) followed, and its title track, along with "Me equivocaría otra vez," cemented Cabrales as a major figure in mainstream Spanish rock. The band's catalogue appeared on DRO, part of the Warner group.

Collaboration has been a recurring thread. In 2008 Cabrales joined Argentine songwriter Andrés Calamaro on "Whisky barato" for the duets record 2 son multitud. Antes de que cuente diez (2009) kept the Raya-produced blend of rock, rhythm and blues and ballads. Its era also produced singles such as "Los huesos de los besos" and "Me acordé de ti." Huyendo conmigo de mí (2014) was led by "Entre la espada y la pared" and showed a more reflective, mature songwriter. That same year the band released a live recording from Bilbao's Teatro Arriaga, which included the song "Cerca de las vías." In 2015 came a special edition recorded at Madrid's Las Ventas bullring.

Critics and audiences have generally credited Fito y Fitipaldis with bringing an earthy, classic rock and roll sensibility to the top of the Spanish charts. Cabrales's plain-spoken lyrics, full of street imagery, everyday love and self-deprecation, connect the rock urbano tradition with a broad pop audience. His records have regularly topped Spanish sales charts, and his tours fill arenas and bullrings across Spain.

The band returned with Cada vez cadáver in 2021 and continues to tour. Its legacy rests on proving that a veteran of the Basque rock underground could reinvent himself without abandoning his roots. Along the way Cabrales built a catalogue of songs that have become standards for a generation of Spanish rock listeners.
1tZ99AnqyjgrmPwLfGU5eo.title: Fito y Fitipaldis

20qISvAhX20dpIbOOzGK3q.extract:
Nasir Jones, known professionally as Nas, was born in Brooklyn in 1973 and raised in the Queensbridge Houses in Long Island City, Queens — at the time the largest public housing development in North America and a fertile breeding ground for hip-hop talent following the success of Marley Marl and the Juice Crew. The son of jazz cornetist Olu Dara, Nas dropped out of school in the eighth grade and immersed himself in the local rap scene, drawing inspiration from Queensbridge predecessors like MC Shan and Roxanne Shanté, as well as Rakim's lyrical dexterity. His first appearance came in 1991 on Main Source's "Live at the Barbeque," produced by Large Professor, where his opening verse made him an immediate object of fascination among New York rap insiders.

That buzz culminated in his 1994 debut album Illmatic, released on Columbia Records, which assembled an unprecedented roster of producers — DJ Premier, Pete Rock, Q-Tip, Large Professor, and L.E.S. — across a tight ten tracks. Songs like "N.Y. State of Mind," "The World Is Yours," "Life's a Bitch" (featuring AZ and a trumpet solo from his father), and "One Love" set a new bar for street poetry, and the album is now routinely cited as one of the greatest hip-hop records ever made. His follow-up, It Was Written (1996), produced largely by Trackmasters, pivoted toward a more commercial, mafioso-rap aesthetic and yielded the hit "If I Ruled the World (Imagine That)" with Lauryn Hill, going multi-platinum despite a more divided critical reception.

The late 1990s and early 2000s saw Nas form the short-lived supergroup The Firm with AZ, Foxy Brown, and Nature, and release a string of albums including I Am... (1999), Nastradamus (1999), and Stillmatic (2001). The latter was widely seen as a creative resurgence, fueled in part by his high-profile feud with Jay-Z, whose "Takeover" Nas answered with the scorching "Ether." He continued with God's Son (2002) and the double album Street's Disciple (2004), then signed to Def Jam — then helmed by Jay-Z — and released Hip Hop Is Dead in 2006, a polemical state-of-the-genre record. His 2008 untitled album, originally announced under a more incendiary title, tackled race in America directly on tracks like "Sly Fox" and "Black President."

Nas's collaborative 2010 album with reggae artist Damian Marley, Distant Relatives, channeled proceeds toward African charities and broadened his thematic range. After Life Is Good (2012), a reflective record built around his divorce from singer Kelis, he entered a prolific late-career phase working extensively with Kanye West, who produced the seven-track Nasir (2018) as part of the Wyoming sessions, and Hit-Boy, with whom he made the King's Disease trilogy (2020–2022) and Magic series. King's Disease won him his first competitive Grammy for Best Rap Album in 2021, after decades of nominations.

Beyond music, Nas co-founded the venture capital firm QueensBridge Venture Partners, with early investments in Ridesharing, Dropbox, and Coinbase, and launched the Mass Appeal media and record label. He remains an active recording artist and a defining figure of East Coast hip-hop, his Queensbridge origins and Illmatic-era verses still serving as a touchstone for lyrical craft in rap.
20qISvAhX20dpIbOOzGK3q.title: Nas

22bE4uQ6baNwSHPVcDxLCe.extract:
The Rolling Stones formed in London in 1962, emerging from the city's burgeoning rhythm and blues club scene centered on venues like the Ealing Jazz Club and the Crawdaddy Club in Richmond. Active for more than six decades, they rank among the longest-running and most successful bands in rock history, outlasting nearly all of their British Invasion contemporaries.

The band's core came together when childhood acquaintances Mick Jagger and Keith Richards reconnected on a Dartford railway platform in 1961, bonding over records by Chuck Berry and Muddy Waters, whose song "Rollin' Stone" gave the group its name. Guitarist Brian Jones, a devoted blues purist, founded the group and recruited pianist Ian Stewart. Bassist Bill Wyman and drummer Charlie Watts completed the classic lineup by early 1963. Encouraged by Alexis Korner's Blues Incorporated, a key incubator for London's blues scene, the band built a following before manager Andrew Loog Oldham signed them to Decca Records in the UK, with London Records handling American releases. Oldham also produced their early recordings and cultivated their image as a scruffy, menacing counterpoint to the Beatles.

Their early output leaned heavily on covers. The 1964 debut The Rolling Stones (issued in the US as England's Newest Hitmakers) featured songs by Bo Diddley, Willie Dixon, and Slim Harpo, while the Five by Five EP and 12 X 5 captured sessions at Chicago's Chess Studios, the home of their idols. Oldham pushed Jagger and Richards to write their own material, and the payoff arrived with "The Last Time" and especially "(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction," whose fuzz-toned Richards riff powered Out Of Our Heads in 1965 to international success. Aftermath (1966) was their first album consisting entirely of Jagger-Richards originals, with Jones adding sitar to "Paint It, Black" and marimba and dulcimer elsewhere, signaling a broadening palette. Later landmarks included Beggars Banquet (1968), Let It Bleed (1969), Sticky Fingers (1971), and Exile on Main St. (1972), several produced by Jimmy Miller, with tracks like "Sympathy for the Devil," "Gimme Shelter," and "Brown Sugar."

The lineup shifted over the years. Jones was dismissed in 1969 and died weeks later, replaced by Mick Taylor, who in turn gave way to Ronnie Wood in 1975. In 1970 the band launched their own Rolling Stones Records with its famous tongue-and-lips logo. Their era was shadowed by drug arrests and the 1969 Altamont concert, where a fan was killed during their set, an event documented in the film Gimme Shelter.

Critics have long regarded the band's late-sixties and early-seventies run as one of rock's greatest stretches, and they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1989. Their stadium tours set attendance and revenue records repeatedly, establishing the template for the modern rock spectacle.

Charlie Watts died in 2021, with Steve Jordan taking over on drums for touring. In 2023 the band released Hackney Diamonds, their first album of original material since 2005's A Bigger Bang, produced by Andrew Watt and featuring Paul McCartney, Elton John, Lady Gaga, and Stevie Wonder. It earned a Grammy for Best Rock Album, and Jagger, Richards, and Wood continue to tour.
22bE4uQ6baNwSHPVcDxLCe.title: The Rolling Stones

24Wa5wIZIo1sPkzVGP0B5p.extract:
Pete Townshend was born on 19 May 1945 in Chiswick, west London, to a musical family. His father Cliff played saxophone with the RAF dance band the Squadronaires and his mother Betty was a singer. Raised in Acton, he attended Acton County Grammar School alongside John Entwistle and later studied at Ealing Art College. That art-school environment exposed him to auto-destructive art theory, which fed directly into his guitar-smashing stage act. Although he is best known as the principal songwriter and guitarist of the Who, whom he has led since the mid-1960s, he has maintained a parallel solo career stretching from the early 1970s to the present.

The Who grew out of the Detours, a band fronted by Roger Daltrey. With Keith Moon on drums, they briefly became the High Numbers before settling on their permanent name under managers Kit Lambert and Chris Stamp. They became the house band of the London mod scene. Townshend's formative influences ranged from American R&B and Link Wray to jazz. From 1967 onward he was also shaped by the teachings of the Indian spiritual master Meher Baba, whose influence runs through Tommy, Lifehouse, and much of his solo work.

His first widely released solo album, Who Came First (1972), grew out of devotional records he had made for Baba followers. It mixed home demos such as "Pure and Easy" and "Let's See Action" with Ronnie Lane's "Evolution" and a cover of Jim Reeves' "There's a Heartache Following Me." Rough Mix (1977), a duet album with Lane produced by Glyn Johns, featured Eric Clapton, Charlie Watts and John Entwistle. Its looser, rootsier sound shows on tracks like "Street in the City" and "My Baby Gives It Away." Empty Glass (1980), produced by Chris Thomas and released in the US on Atco, was his commercial peak. It included "Let My Love Open the Door," a US top ten hit, along with "Rough Boys" and "A Little Is Enough." Thomas also produced the denser All The Best Cowboys Have Chinese Eyes (1982), which included "Slit Skirts." The Scoop series (1983, 1987, 1994) gathered demos that revealed how fully he sketched Who songs at home.

The mid-1980s brought more conceptual projects. White City: A Novel (1985) arrived with an accompanying film and the single "Face the Face." Deep End Live! (1986) documented a big-band touring ensemble that included David Gilmour. The Iron Man (1989), adapted from Ted Hughes' children's story, featured John Lee Hooker and Nina Simone. Psychoderelict (1993) was a radio-play-style concept album about an aging rock star. That same year, the Broadway production of The Who's Tommy won Tony Awards, including one for Townshend's score. The stage work later spawned international productions such as the German-language recording released in 2015. Also in 2015, Classic Quadrophenia recast his 1973 rock opera orchestrally, with Alfie Boe singing the lead.

Critics have long regarded Townshend as one of rock's most ambitious songwriters. He is credited with popularizing the rock opera and pioneering feedback, power chords and the windmill guitar style. Players from Paul Weller to the punk generation have cited him as an influence. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with the Who in 1990 and received Kennedy Center Honors in 2008.

Townshend published his memoir, Who I Am, in 2012 and his first novel, The Age of Anxiety, in 2019. That same year he and Daltrey released the Who album WHO, and he has continued to tour with the band. His legacy rests both on the Who's canon and on a solo body of work that exposes the more intimate, searching side of his writing.
24Wa5wIZIo1sPkzVGP0B5p.title: Pete Townshend

267VY6GX5LyU5c9M85ECZQ.extract:
Dinosaur Jr. emerged from Amherst, Massachusetts in 1984, formed by guitarist and singer J Mascis, bassist Lou Barlow, and drummer Murph (Emmett Jefferson Murphy III). Mascis and Barlow had previously played together in the hardcore band Deep Wound, and when that group dissolved, Mascis pivoted toward something slower, heavier, and more melodic, drawing on his love of Neil Young, Black Sabbath, the Stooges, and the loud-and-tuneful template of Hüsker Dü. The band initially called itself simply Dinosaur, adding the "Jr." after a lawsuit threat from a group of veteran musicians using the same name.

Their self-titled 1985 debut on Homestead Records was a rough, eclectic introduction, but it was 1987's You're Living All Over Me, also on Homestead, that crystallized their sound: shredded ear-bleeding guitar solos, mumbled vocals, and a fragile sweetness buried under feedback. The follow-up, Bug (1988, SST Records), included the signature track "Freak Scene" and the harrowing "Don't" on which Barlow screams himself raw. Tensions between Mascis and Barlow boiled over after Bug, and Barlow was ousted, going on to form Sebadoh and later Folk Implosion. Murph and Mascis carried on, signing to Sire/Warner Bros. and releasing Green Mind in 1991, which was largely a Mascis solo effort, followed by Where You Been (1993), the band's commercial peak, which yielded the alt-rock radio staple "Start Choppin'."

Through the mid-1990s the lineup shifted around Mascis as the sole constant; Without a Sound (1994) produced the single "Feel the Pain," whose Spike Jonze-directed video became an MTV fixture during the alternative boom. By the time of Hand It Over (1997), Murph had departed and the band's commercial momentum had faded; Mascis put the project on ice and worked under his own name and with the band the Fog. Throughout this run, Dinosaur Jr. were touchstones for the indie and grunge worlds, frequently cited by Kurt Cobain and Kevin Shields as influential, and they shared scenes and bills with peers like Sonic Youth, Mudhoney, and the Pixies.

The band's most surprising act was its reunion. In 2005, Mascis, Barlow, and Murph reconvened the original lineup, signed to Merge Records, and released Beyond in 2007 — the kind of late-career return that confounded expectations by being genuinely strong rather than nostalgic. They followed it with Farm (2009), I Bet on Sky (2012), Give a Glimpse of What Yer Not (2016), and Sweep It Into Space (2021), the last co-produced with Kurt Vile. The reunited trio has now been active for longer than the original incarnation, touring consistently and releasing records at a steady clip.

Critically, Dinosaur Jr. are regarded as foundational to American indie rock and a crucial bridge between 1980s hardcore and 1990s alternative, with Mascis frequently named among the most distinctive guitarists of his generation for his Marshall-stacked, melodic, classic-rock-indebted soloing. Their early SST-era records remain canonical reference points cited by artists from My Bloody Valentine to Built to Spill to Snail Mail, and the band's unlikely second act has only solidified their reputation as one of the most durable and influential groups of the post-punk era.
267VY6GX5LyU5c9M85ECZQ.title: Dinosaur Jr.

26VFTg2z8YR0cCuwLzESi2.extract:
Halsey, born Ashley Nicolette Frangipane in 1994 in Edison, New Jersey, emerged from the same loose ecosystem of internet-bred alt-pop artists who broke through in the mid-2010s via SoundCloud, Tumblr, and viral YouTube covers. Of mixed Italian, Hungarian, and African American heritage, she spent her teenage years bouncing between New Jersey and New York, busking in Manhattan and absorbing an eclectic diet of Brand New, The Weeknd, Lana Del Rey, and Bring Me the Horizon. The stage name Halsey is famously an anagram of her first name and a nod to the Halsey Street stop on the New York subway. After a viral acoustic response to The Chainsmokers and a buzzy presence at SXSW, she signed with Astralwerks in 2014.

Her debut EP Room 93 arrived in late 2014, establishing the cinematic, blue-lit synth-pop aesthetic that would define her early work. The full-length Badlands followed in 2015, a loosely conceptual record set in a dystopian landscape and built around tracks like Castle, New Americana, and Colors. It hit the top three of the Billboard 200 and turned her into one of the dominant voices of post-Lorde alt-pop. Her profile exploded in 2016 when she featured on The Chainsmokers' Closer, a global number one that spent twelve weeks atop the Hot 100 and made her ubiquitous on pop radio, even as parts of her fanbase grumbled about the mainstream pivot.

Hopeless Fountain Kingdom in 2017, loosely inspired by Romeo and Juliet, debuted at number one and contained Bad at Love and the Quavo-featuring Lie, while Now or Never showcased her continuing fluency in dark, R&B-tinged pop. In 2019, the standalone single Without Me, a confessional kiss-off interpolating Justin Timberlake's Cry Me a River, became her first solo number one and remains her commercial peak. Manic, released in January 2020, was a more genre-promiscuous and autobiographical statement, weaving in country (Finally // beautiful stranger), pop-punk-adjacent material (929, 3am), and interludes featuring Alanis Morissette, Dominic Fike, and SUGA of BTS, with whom she had previously collaborated on Boy with Luv.

The most striking turn came in 2021 with If I Can't Have Love, I Want Power, produced entirely by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross of Nine Inch Nails. Written during her pregnancy with her son Ender, the album fused industrial, grunge, and gothic chamber-pop in a way few major-label pop stars would attempt, drawing strong critical reviews and earning her some of the most serious artistic notices of her career. Throughout this period she has also been a vocal advocate for reproductive rights, endometriosis awareness, and bisexual visibility, and she published the poetry collection I Would Leave Me If I Could in 2020.

In 2024 Halsey announced she had been diagnosed with lupus and a rare T-cell disorder, framing the single The End and the subsequent album The Great Impersonator around that experience; the record leans into pastiche, with songs styled after artists who influenced her, from Fiona Apple to Stevie Nicks. Now signed to Columbia after her Capitol/Astralwerks tenure, she remains one of the more restless and stylistically mobile pop stars of her generation, an artist whose legacy is likely to rest as much on her willingness to detonate her own commercial template as on the hits themselves.
26VFTg2z8YR0cCuwLzESi2.title: Halsey

2AV6XDIs32ofIJhkkDevjm.extract:
Curtis Mayfield was born on June 3, 1942, in Chicago, Illinois, and grew up in the city's Cabrini-Green housing projects. He became one of the defining voices of Chicago soul, active from the late 1950s until shortly before his death on December 26, 1999. Raised partly by his grandmother, a spiritualist minister, he absorbed gospel music in church and taught himself guitar in an unusual open F-sharp tuning, which gave his playing its distinctive, chiming quality.

As a teenager Mayfield joined his friend Jerry Butler in a gospel group. The two then joined Sam Gooden and brothers Arthur and Richard Brooks in the Roosters, who became the Impressions. Their 1958 hit "For Your Precious Love" launched Butler's solo career. Mayfield stayed on as the group's chief songwriter and lead voice. Working with arranger Johnny Pate on ABC-Paramount, the Impressions produced a run of gospel-tinged hits that became anthems of the civil rights movement, among them "Gypsy Woman," "It's All Right," "Keep On Pushing," "People Get Ready," "We're a Winner," and "Choice of Colors." Mayfield also wrote and produced for other artists, including Major Lance and Gene Chandler, and he founded the labels Windy C, Mayfield, and Curtom, the last with partner Eddie Thomas.

Mayfield left the Impressions in 1970 and released his solo debut, Curtis, on Curtom. The album paired funk grooves with orchestral arrangements and pointed social commentary on tracks such as "(Don't Worry) If There's a Hell Below, We're All Going to Go" and the exuberant "Move On Up." Roots and the concert album Curtis/Live! followed in 1971. His commercial peak came with the 1972 soundtrack to Gordon Parks Jr.'s film Super Fly. Its songs "Freddie's Dead" and "Superfly" were both major hits, and they critiqued the drug trade rather than glamorizing it. The album topped the Billboard pop chart and outsold the film's box office. Later albums, including Back to the World, Sweet Exorcist, Got to Find a Way, and There's No Place Like America Today, continued his socially conscious soul. By the late 1970s, on records like Never Say You Can't Survive and Do It All Night, he leaned toward the disco era.

Through Curtom, Mayfield wrote and produced soundtracks for other performers as well. These included Claudine for Gladys Knight & the Pips, Sparkle for Aretha Franklin, and Let's Do It Again for the Staple Singers, whose title track reached number one. He also scored the 1977 film Short Eyes, in which he appeared on screen.

On August 13, 1990, a lighting rig fell on Mayfield during an outdoor concert in Brooklyn and left him paralyzed from the neck down. He kept working anyway, recording his final album, New World Order (1996), by singing lying down, often a line at a time. Tribute projects drew artists such as Bruce Springsteen, Eric Clapton, and Lenny Kravitz. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame twice, with the Impressions in 1991 and as a solo artist in 1999, and he received a Grammy Legend Award.

Mayfield died in Roswell, Georgia, in 1999, from complications of diabetes. His legacy endures in his songwriting, his model of artist-owned labels, and his falsetto-driven protest soul. Hip-hop producers have sampled his work extensively, and "People Get Ready" and "Move On Up" remain standards of American music.
2AV6XDIs32ofIJhkkDevjm.title: Curtis Mayfield

2DaxqgrOhkeH0fpeiQq2f4.extract:
Oasis emerged from Manchester, England in 1991, forming in the wake of the city's Madchester scene that had produced the Stone Roses and Happy Mondays. The band coalesced around vocalist Liam Gallagher, who joined an existing group called The Rain alongside guitarist Paul "Bonehead" Arthurs, bassist Paul "Guigsy" McGuigan, and drummer Tony McCarroll. The pivotal moment came when Liam's older brother Noel Gallagher, then a roadie for Inspiral Carpets, agreed to join as lead guitarist and principal songwriter on the condition that he would have total creative control. Their formative influences were worn on their sleeve: the Beatles above all, but also the Sex Pistols, T. Rex, the Kinks, and the swagger of the Stone Roses. A now-mythologized 1993 gig at King Tut's Wah Wah Hut in Glasgow led to Creation Records boss Alan McGee signing them almost immediately.

Their 1994 debut Definitely Maybe, produced largely by Owen Morris and Noel Gallagher after earlier sessions with Dave Batchelor were scrapped, became the fastest-selling debut album in British history at the time. Singles like Supersonic, Shakermaker, Live Forever, and Cigarettes & Alcohol distilled a working-class optimism into anthemic, distortion-drenched rock that felt like a corrective to American grunge's introspection. The album's success positioned them as figureheads of Britpop alongside Blur, Suede, and Pulp, and the manufactured chart battle between Oasis's Roll With It and Blur's Country House in August 1995 became a defining tabloid spectacle of the era.

(What's The Story) Morning Glory?, released in October 1995 and again produced with Owen Morris, catapulted them to global stardom. Wonderwall, Don't Look Back In Anger, and Some Might Say turned the band into a cultural phenomenon, and their two nights at Knebworth in August 1996, playing to roughly 250,000 people across the weekend from a ticket demand of over two million, remain a high-water mark for British rock as mass event. The follow-up Be Here Now in 1997, trailed by the sprawling single D'You Know What I Mean? and later Stand By Me and All Around The World, initially sold in enormous quantities but was quickly reassessed as bloated and cocaine-addled, a verdict Noel himself later endorsed.

The late 1990s saw significant lineup upheaval, with Bonehead and Guigsy departing in 1999, replaced eventually by Gem Archer and Andy Bell, while Zak Starkey and later Chris Sharrock took on drumming duties. Albums like Standing on the Shoulder of Giants, Heathen Chemistry, Don't Believe the Truth, and Dig Out Your Soul saw them regain some critical footing without ever recapturing their mid-90s ubiquity. The Gallagher brothers' famously combustible relationship finally destroyed the band backstage at the Rock en Seine festival in Paris on 28 August 2009, when Noel quit citing one confrontation too many with Liam.

For fifteen years the two pursued parallel careers, Noel with the High Flying Birds and Liam with Beady Eye and then a successful solo run, while consistently ruling out reconciliation. That changed in August 2024, when Oasis announced a reunion tour for 2025 spanning the UK, Ireland, and further international dates, prompting a chaotic ticket sale that drew regulatory scrutiny over dynamic pricing. Their legacy is inseparable from Britpop itself: a band whose best songs became civic hymns sung on football terraces and at weddings, and whose influence remains audible in generations of British guitar acts from Kasabian to Blossoms.
2DaxqgrOhkeH0fpeiQq2f4.title: Oasis

2QOIawHpSlOwXDvSqQ9YJR.extract:
Antonio Vivaldi was born on 4 March 1678 in Venice, then the capital of a still-glamorous if declining maritime republic, and died in Vienna on 28 July 1741. He is the central figure of the Italian Baroque concerto, and his active career spanned roughly from the first years of the eighteenth century to the late 1730s. Spotify catalogues his music under the italian baroque, baroque, early music and classical genres. His presence there consists largely of modern performances gathered into compilations such as Vivaldi: The Four Seasons (Remastered) and the many seasonal classical anthologies issued in 2026.

His first teacher was his father, Giovanni Battista Vivaldi, a barber turned professional violinist at St Mark's Basilica. Antonio trained for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703. His red hair earned him the nickname il Prete Rosso, the Red Priest. He soon stopped saying Mass, citing a chronic chest ailment, and that same year began working at the Ospedale della Pietà, a Venetian institution for foundling girls whose all-female orchestra and choir became famous across Europe. Vivaldi served there as violin master and later in broader musical roles for much of his life. The Pietà gave him a resident ensemble on which to test an enormous output of concertos.

His reputation spread through printed collections published in Amsterdam by Estienne Roger. L'estro armonico, Op. 3 (1711), set out his concise three-movement form with bold ritornellos and virtuosic solo episodes, and it became one of the most influential publications of the age. La stravaganza, Op. 4, followed. Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione, Op. 8 (1725), contained the four violin concertos known as The Four Seasons, which are paired with descriptive sonnets and dedicated to the Bohemian Count Wenzel von Morzin. La cetra, Op. 9 (1727), was dedicated to Emperor Charles VI. Alongside these he wrote sacred works including the Gloria RV 589, the Stabat Mater and the oratorio Juditha triumphans (1716). He was also a prolific opera composer and impresario, beginning with Ottone in villa at Vicenza in 1713 and including Orlando furioso (1727) and Griselda (1735), whose libretto was revised by the young Carlo Goldoni.

His career extended well beyond Venice. From 1718 to 1720 he served Prince Philip of Hesse-Darmstadt at Mantua. His long association with the contralto Anna Girò, a frequent star of his operas, drew gossip. His most consequential admirer was Johann Sebastian Bach, who transcribed several of his concertos for keyboard. These include the Concerto for Four Harpsichords BWV 1065, adapted from Op. 3 No. 10. Through such arrangements, Vivaldi's ritornello procedures shaped the German concerto.

Taste in Venice moved on, and Vivaldi travelled to Vienna, apparently hoping for imperial patronage. Charles VI died soon after his arrival, and Vivaldi himself died there in poverty. For nearly two centuries he was remembered mainly through Bach. Revival came in the 1920s, when large manuscript collections were acquired by the National Library in Turin and studied by Alberto Gentili. Alfredo Casella followed with a Vivaldi week in Siena in 1939. Peter Ryom's catalogue later gave the works their standard RV numbers.

Postwar recordings made Vivaldi ubiquitous, notably I Musici's 1955 Four Seasons and Nigel Kennedy's 1989 version with the English Chamber Orchestra, which became one of the best-selling classical records ever. Period-instrument ensembles such as Il Giardino Armonico and Fabio Biondi's Europa Galante have since reshaped how he is heard. The Vivaldi Edition on the Naïve label has brought his neglected operas and sacred music back into circulation. Today The Four Seasons is among the most performed and recorded works in the classical repertoire, and its steady stream of reissues and compilations shows how far his music has travelled from the Pietà.
2QOIawHpSlOwXDvSqQ9YJR.title: Antonio Vivaldi

2QoU3awHVdcHS8LrZEKvSM.extract:
Wilco emerged from Belleville, Illinois in 1994, formed in the immediate aftermath of the breakup of pioneering alt-country band Uncle Tupelo. When Jay Farrar left to form Son Volt, his Uncle Tupelo bandmate Jeff Tweedy gathered the remaining members—bassist John Stirratt, drummer Ken Coomer, and multi-instrumentalist Max Johnston—and added guitarist Jay Bennett shortly thereafter, christening the new outfit Wilco. They signed to Reprise Records, a Warner Bros. subsidiary, and slotted into the burgeoning mid-1990s alt-country scene alongside contemporaries like Whiskeytown, the Jayhawks, and Son Volt, with the magazine No Depression more or less treating them as flagship artists of the movement.

Their 1995 debut A.M. was a relatively straightforward roots-rock record, but Wilco's ambitions quickly outgrew the genre. The 1996 double album Being There expanded their palette toward Stones-y rock, power pop, and lo-fi experimentation, and 1999's Summerteeth pushed further still, layering Brian Wilson-indebted harmonies, Mellotrons, and studio textures over Tweedy's increasingly dark lyrics. During this period the band also collaborated with British folk legend Billy Bragg on Mermaid Avenue (1998) and Mermaid Avenue Vol. II (2000), setting unpublished Woody Guthrie lyrics to new music—projects that significantly raised their profile and earned a Grammy nomination.

The band's defining moment came with Yankee Hotel Foxtrot, recorded with engineer/collaborator Jim O'Rourke and famously rejected by Reprise, who dropped the band; Wilco streamed the album free online before Nonesuch, another Warner imprint, picked it up and released it in 2002. The record's fractured pop, tape-loop interludes, and songs like "I Am Trying to Break Your Heart," "Jesus, Etc.," and "Heavy Metal Drummer" earned widespread acclaim and a documentary, I Am Trying to Break Your Heart, directed by Sam Jones. Jay Bennett was dismissed during the album's making, and the band's lineup churned further before stabilizing with the arrival of guitarist Nels Cline and multi-instrumentalist Pat Sansone around 2004. A Ghost Is Born (2004), again featuring O'Rourke, won Grammys for Best Alternative Music Album and Best Recording Package.

From Sky Blue Sky (2007) onward, Wilco settled into a remarkably stable six-piece lineup—Tweedy, Stirratt, Cline, Sansone, drummer Glenn Kotche, and keyboardist Mikael Jorgensen—and a more relaxed, classic-rock-leaning sound, while still indulging experimental impulses on records like Wilco (The Album), The Whole Love, and the surprise-released Star Wars (2015). They launched their own label, dBpm Records, and since 2005 have curated the Solid Sound Festival at MASS MoCA in North Adams, Massachusetts, an event that doubles as a showcase for Tweedy's and the members' wide-ranging side projects.

Critically, Wilco have long been treated as one of America's most important rock bands of their generation, frequently compared to a latter-day version of acts like the Band or Big Star for the way they fuse traditional songcraft with restless studio experimentation. Tweedy has also pursued a productive solo and memoir-writing career, releasing the autobiography Let's Go (So We Can Get Back) in 2018. The group remains active, having released Cruel Country in 2022 and Cousin, produced by Cate Le Bon, in 2023, and continues to tour and record without any apparent intention of slowing down.
2QoU3awHVdcHS8LrZEKvSM.title: Wilco

2UDplVRprMbazU74Hq8OLl.extract:
The Jayhawks formed in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in 1985, emerging from the same Twin Cities scene that produced the Replacements and Hüsker Dü, though their sound pointed toward country and folk rather than punk. Built around the songwriting partnership of Mark Olson and Gary Louris, with bassist Marc Perlman as a constant presence, the band has remained active in various configurations for nearly four decades. Alongside Uncle Tupelo, they are widely regarded as foundational figures in what came to be called alternative country.

Olson founded the group with Perlman and drummer Norm Rogers, and Louris joined shortly after. Louris brought a rock guitarist's instincts to Olson's love of traditional country, and the two quickly built their sound on close two-part harmonies indebted to Gram Parsons, the Flying Burrito Brothers, and the Everly Brothers. Their self-titled debut, often called The Bunkhouse Album, appeared in 1986 on a small local label. It was followed in 1989 by Blue Earth on Twin/Tone Records, a sparse, rustic set that sharpened the Olson-Louris vocal blend.

Their breakthrough came by chance. While Twin/Tone's Dave Ayers was on hold on the phone with Def American producer George Drakoulias, Drakoulias heard Blue Earth playing in the background and soon signed the band. Drakoulias produced Hollywood Town Hall (1992), which paired the harmonies with fuller, Neil Young-inflected electric arrangements on songs like "Waiting for the Sun" and "Settled Down Like Rain." Keyboardist Karen Grotberg joined for Tomorrow the Green Grass (1995), a warmer, more polished record featuring "Blue," which became their best-known song. Olson left the band later that year, moving to California to make music with his wife, Victoria Williams.

Louris took over as principal songwriter, and the band's sound changed under him. Sound of Lies (1997) was darker and more psychedelic, shaped by personal turmoil. Smile (2000), produced by Bob Ezrin, pushed toward glossy pop and included "I'm Gonna Make You Love Me." Rainy Day Music (2003), produced by Ethan Johns and released on Lost Highway, returned to acoustic textures and Byrds-like jangle, with drummer Tim O'Reagan contributing songs and vocals. A hiatus followed. Olson and Louris reunited as a duo, then rejoined the full band for Mockingbird Time (2011), released on Rounder. Olson departed again afterward.

Critics have consistently praised the band, and Tomorrow the Green Grass is frequently listed among the essential Americana albums of the 1990s. Its influence runs through later roots-rock acts that adopted their blend of harmony vocals and jangling guitars. A Legacy Edition of Tomorrow the Green Grass, along with expanded reissues of Hollywood Town Hall, Sound of Lies, and Rainy Day Music, has invited fresh appraisal of their catalog, particularly the overlooked Louris-led records.

The Louris-led lineup with Perlman, O'Reagan, and Grotberg returned with Paging Mr. Proust (2016), co-produced by Peter Buck and Tucker Martine. They later served as the backing band on Ray Davies' Americana project, then released Back Roads and Abandoned Motels (2018) and XOXO (2020). The Jayhawks continue to tour and record, a durable link between the Minneapolis underground and the broader Americana tradition.
2UDplVRprMbazU74Hq8OLl.title: The Jayhawks

2VAvhf61GgLYmC6C8anyX1.extract:
Boards of Canada are a Scottish electronic duo composed of brothers Michael Sandison and Marcus Eoin, based for much of their career in rural Pendland, near Edinburgh. Active since the late 1980s, though they only began releasing music publicly in the mid-1990s, the pair became central figures in the wave of melodic, texture-focused electronic music that emerged from the United Kingdom in the wake of Aphex Twin and Autechre. They took their name from the National Film Board of Canada, whose educational documentaries from the 1970s — with their grainy film stock, synthesizer scores, and earnest narration — shaped the nostalgic, slightly uncanny atmosphere that would define their sound.

The brothers grew up partly in Canada before settling in Scotland, and as teenagers played in a larger collective called Hexagon Sun, which later became the name of their home studio and informal creative circle. Their earliest self-released cassettes and the limited 1996 EP Twoism circulated in small numbers before catching the attention of Sean Booth of Autechre, who helped bring them to the Skam label in Manchester. Their Skam EP Hi Scores in 1996 established the template: warm, detuned analog synthesizers, hip-hop-derived broken beats, half-buried children's voices, and melodies that felt simultaneously sunlit and decayed.

Their debut full-length, Music Has the Right to Children, was released in 1998 jointly by Warp and Skam and became one of the defining electronic albums of its era. Tracks like Roygbiv, Aquarius, and Turquoise Hexagon Sun cemented an aesthetic that critics often described as hauntological years before that term entered wider music writing.
